You're right. My previous revision fixed the prose, but two emit labels still said "grey blocks" when they meant the cyan (8) blocks. In this version I changed only the literal text inside those two labels, from "grey" to "cyan".

- No label names magenta (6) by word. The per-block label shows the colour as a number through the formatted expression `{c}`, and I left that expression unchanged.
- All code is identical to before. That includes the code comments, which still say "grey" but refer to the cyan (8) cells.

## How the puzzle works

**What the grid is made of.** Each input has two parts:
- **A legend on the left.** It is a row of full-height vertical lines in distinct colours, separated by black (0) background columns. In pair 1 these are blue (1), magenta (6) and orange (7).
- **A canvas of cyan (8) cells on the right.** It is built from solid rectangles placed edge to edge, left to right. Two rectangles can touch and form one connected component. In pair 1, the 2×4 cyan block at columns 10–11 and the 3×3 cyan block at columns 12–14 merge into a single 17-cell object. So connectivity is not the right way to split them.

**What the output does.**
1. The legend lines are erased to black background.
2. Each cyan rectangle is recoloured with one legend colour. The k-th rectangle from the left gets the k-th legend line from the left.

Checking this against the pairs:
- **Pair 1:** the legend is blue, magenta, orange (1, 6, 7). The blocks are cols 7–9 → blue, cols 10–11 → magenta, cols 12–14 → orange. This matches the output.
- **Pair 2:** the legend is yellow, green, red (4, 3, 2). The blocks are cols 8–11 → yellow, cols 12–13 → green, cols 15–18 → red. This matches.
- **Pair 3:** the legend is green, red, yellow, orange (3, 2, 4, 7). The blocks are cols 9–10, 11–12, 14–15 and 16–17, which get green, red, yellow and orange in that order. This matches.

**How to split touching rectangles.** I scan the cyan area column by column. Each column with cyan has a set of cyan rows, and a rectangle is a maximal run of adjacent columns sharing exactly the same set. A new rectangle starts whenever the set changes or a column has no cyan. Pair 1 shows why this works: column 10 has cyan in rows 2–5 and column 12 has cyan in rows 0–2, so a new block begins at 12 even though the cells touch.

**The test input.** The legend is blue, green, red, yellow, magenta, orange (1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 7), six lines in all. The cyan column runs are:

| Columns | Cyan rows | New colour |
|---|---|---|
| 13–15 | 0–2 | blue (1) |
| 16–17 | 3–6 | green (3) |
| 18–19 | 1–3 | red (2) |
| 20–22 | 0–1 | yellow (4) |
| 23–25 | 2–6 | magenta (6) |
| 26–27 | 1–4 | orange (7) |

That gives six blocks for six legend colours, so the counts agree.

**Teaching stages.** The program records these canvases:
1. The legend erased.
2. One canvas after each cyan rectangle is recoloured.
3. The final canvas.
